cvs: 'Charity' – spreading sprays, the classic · 'Lionel Fortescue' – very upright, longer sprays · 'Buckland' – longer, arching sprays
foliage: evergreen; large pinnate leaves with spiny holly-like leaflets, sometimes reddish in cold weather
hardinessNote: Hardy in a cold winter throughout most of the UK, approximately -15 to -10°C.
prune: Little needed. After flowering, cut leggy stems back to a leaf rosette to keep it bushy; old bare plants can be cut back hard in spring.
resilience: Tough, shade-tolerant evergreen that copes with clay and dry shade once established. Flowers in winter when little else does. Pests: occasional mahonia rust and leaf-spot, mostly cosmetic.
toxicity: Leaflets carry sharp spines, so wear gloves when handling. Berries and roots contain berberine and may cause a mild stomach upset if a child eats many; the ASPCA lists common Mahonia as safe for dogs and cats.
uncertain: peak: retailers and RHS retail page give Nov–Mar; Nov-Feb kept to match the deck's Charity and Lionel Fortescue cards
spread: RHS profile 1.5–2.5 m; many sellers quote 4 × 4 m — RHS used
raceme habit: RHS says densely clustered, arching; Cambridge Botanic Garden says erect — described as dense upright sprays, matching Oscar's photo
toxicity: no RHS statement; berberine is general to Mahonia; ASPCA listing is for M. aquifolium
compliance: older cultivar (Slieve Donard, 1966), no PBR or Schedule 9 listing found
sunNeed/sunMin/aspect aligned with the deck's other two Mahonia × media cards, not a cultivar-specific source
uses: Winter interest · shady borders · winter food for bees · informal screen or barrier · woodland gardens
visual: Dense upright sprays of scented bright yellow winter flowers · spiny dark green leaves
water: Water regularly in the first year; once established it copes with dry spells, but do not let it dry out in hot summers.
